content: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a clinical syndrome caused by an imbalance in the vaginal microbiota, also referred to as the vaginal flora. The healthy vaginal environment is predominantly maintained by lactobacilli, which are Gram-positive bacilli. These bacteria play a critical role in preserving the health of the female genital tract by maintaining the vaginal pH at normal levels, typically acidic. When the vaginal pH becomes disrupted, certain microorganisms can overgrow, displacing the normal flora. This overgrowth can lead to a low-grade infection, often characterized by abnormal vaginal discharge. Lactobacilli are essential for maintaining the vaginal ecosystem. They produce lactic acid, which helps sustain the acidic pH of the vagina, creating an environment that inhibits the growth of pathogenic organisms. When this balance is disturbed, opportunistic bacteria such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma species, and anaerobes can proliferate, leading to BV. This condition is associated with a thin, white or gray vaginal discharge and an unpleasant odor, particularly noticeable after sexual intercourse. BV must be differentiated from other conditions that can present with similar symptoms, such as trichomoniasis, atrophic vaginitis, desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, vaginal candidiasis, and cervicitis. It is the most common cause of vaginal symptoms in women, although the exact role of sexual activity in its development remains unclear. BV is not considered a sexually transmitted infection, but certain sexual behaviors, such as having multiple or new sexual partners, may increase the risk. Untreated BV can lead to significant complications, including premature delivery, postpartum infections, clinically apparent or subclinical pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and post-surgical complications following procedures like abortion, hysterectomy, or cesarean section. Additionally, BV increases susceptibility to HIV infection and, in some cases, may contribute to infertility. In pregnant women, untreated BV can result in serious pregnancy-related complications, such as premature rupture of membranes, preterm labor, chorioamnionitis, postpartum endometritis, and septic abortion. Antimicrobial therapy is recommended for all symptomatic women and for high-risk asymptomatic pregnant women diagnosed with BV. Metronidazole is the preferred treatment for pregnant patients. Preventive measures include limiting the number of sexual partners, avoiding douching, and using condoms or estrogen-containing contraceptives during sexual activity. Historically, the role of bacterial flora in vaginal infections was first hypothesized by Albert Döderlein in 1892. In 1955, Gardner and Dukes identified Haemophilus vaginalis (later renamed Gardnerella vaginalis) as a causative agent of foul-smelling, watery vaginal discharge. The diagnosis of BV can be made using clinical criteria, such as Amsel’s diagnostic criteria, or through laboratory methods like Gram staining, which is considered the gold standard. Other diagnostic tools include the Affirm VPIII test, chromogenic diagnostic tests (e.g., OSOM BV Blue system), and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Most women with BV are asymptomatic, with 50–75% reporting no symptoms. For those who are symptomatic, the most common complaints include a thin, white or gray vaginal discharge and a fishy vaginal odor, especially after sexual activity. A thorough sexual history is essential for diagnosis, focusing on the number and type of sexual partners and any history of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). On physical examination, findings typically include a fishy odor, thin white or gray discharge, and an absence of significant vulvovaginal inflammation. Imaging studies are not associated with the diagnosis of BV. However, laboratory findings, such as the presence of clue cells on microscopy, are diagnostic. Primary prevention strategies for BV include reducing the number of sexual partners, avoiding douching, and using barrier methods like condoms. Additionally, estrogen-containing contraceptives and bacteriotherapy may play a role in prevention. Routine screening for BV in asymptomatic pregnant women is not recommended, as there is insufficient evidence to support its role in preventing preterm birth.
